items.prompt: What does it mean for a microservice to be "independently deployable"?

options.label: It can be released without redeploying other services
It is deployed on a fixed schedule set by the whole system
It must run on its own dedicated physical server
It has no runtime dependency on any other service

rubric: Independent deployability means one service can be released on its own.
Distractors confuse deployment independence with hardware isolation or zero dependencies.

items.prompt: Which component commonly acts as a single entry point that routes external client requests to the right internal services?

options.label: Message broker
API gateway
Service registry
Container image

rubric: An API gateway is the single entry point that routes client requests.
A service registry tracks instance locations and a broker carries messages; neither is the client entry point.

items.prompt: In a typical microservices design, how is data ownership usually arranged?

options.label: Each service owns its data store and exposes it via its API
One dedicated data service holds the records and the others stay stateless
Data is kept in the API gateway's cache and shared by all services
All services read and write one shared central database

rubric: Database-per-service is the standard guidance.
A shared central database is the common anti-pattern that couples services.

items.prompt: Which pattern stops a service from calling a dependency that has failed repeatedly, so the failure does not spread?

options.label: Service registry
Circuit breaker
Sidecar
API composition

rubric: A circuit breaker opens after repeated failures and blocks further calls.
A sidecar is a helper process and does not stop calls to failing services.

items.prompt: Which of these is an example of asynchronous communication between services?

options.label: Invoking a gRPC method and blocking until it returns
Sending an HTTP request to another service's API and holding the connection open for its reply
Calling a REST endpoint and waiting for the response
Publishing an event to a broker and moving on

rubric: Publishing to a broker lets the sender continue without waiting.
REST and gRPC calls that wait are synchronous; direct database queries break service boundaries.

items.prompt: Which of the following are typical characteristics of a microservices architecture? Select all that apply.

options.label: Each service is small and owned by a single team
Services are organised around business capabilities
Every service must be written in the same programming language
The whole system is built and released as one deployable unit

rubric: Microservices are organised around business capabilities and owned by small teams.
A single deployable unit describes a monolith, and a single language is not required.

items.prompt: A team runs many service instances in containers, and instance addresses change whenever containers restart or scale. The order service needs to find the current address of the payment service. Which component is designed to provide this lookup?

options.label: A circuit breaker placed around the payment calls
A service registry used for service discovery
A shared database holding the payment code
A saga coordinator for the payment workflow

rubric: Service discovery via a registry maps service names to live instance addresses.
A circuit breaker handles failures, not lookup, and a saga handles distributed transactions.

items.prompt: Why is it discouraged for several microservices to share one database schema?

options.label: Services running in separate containers usually struggle to reach the same database
Shared databases tend to cost more in licensing than several separate ones
A schema change by one service can break others, coupling them
Databases generally slow down sharply when several applications connect at once

rubric: Shared schemas create hidden coupling, which defeats independent deployment.
The other options state technical or cost limits that are not the real reason.

items.prompt: A web shop's search feature gets ten times more traffic than its checkout. How do microservices help here?

options.label: Each request runs faster because services are smaller than a monolith
Search stays available even if its own service crashes under the load
Only the search service needs more instances, not the whole app
Checkout no longer needs monitoring because search is separate from it

rubric: Services can be scaled individually based on load.
Microservices do not automatically speed up requests or remove failure and monitoring concerns.

items.prompt: The order service publishes an `OrderPlaced` event, and the email and inventory services each react to it on their own. How is this best classified?

options.label: Event-driven asynchronous communication
A shared-database integration between services
A monolithic in-process method call
Synchronous request-response calls between services

rubric: Publishing events that consumers react to independently is event-driven and asynchronous.
Request-response and shared databases involve waiting or direct coupling, which this does not.

items.prompt: Service A calls service B synchronously with no timeout. Service B becomes very slow. What is the most likely result?

options.label: Service B's slowness is hidden from service A
Service A automatically switches to another service
Service A's code is redeployed by the platform
Service A's requests hang and its threads pile up

rubric: Without timeouts, callers wait and exhaust resources, so failures cascade.
Services do not switch or hide failures unless resilience patterns are added.

items.prompt: Why is a saga used for an operation spanning an order service and a payment service?

options.label: It locks one shared table so both services commit together
It chains local transactions and undoes earlier ones on failure
It copies each service's data into the other so both stay in sync
It encrypts messages sent between the two services in transit

rubric: A saga sequences local transactions with compensating actions because one ACID transaction cannot span services.
Locking a shared table breaks service data ownership.

items.prompt: Which of the following are common drawbacks that microservices add compared with a monolith? Select all that apply.

options.label: Data is often only eventually consistent across services
Debugging a request across services is harder
Network calls add latency and can fail
Every change requires redeploying the entire system

rubric: Network failure, harder tracing and eventual consistency are real costs of distribution.
Redeploying everything is a monolith trait, not a microservices drawback.

items.prompt: A team of four is starting a new product whose requirements are still changing weekly. A colleague proposes splitting it into twelve microservices from day one. Which response best reflects why this may be unwise?

options.label: Early boundaries are likely wrong, and running many services is heavy for four people
A monolith can be split later only by a full rewrite, so the split must happen on day one
Microservices need a separate database engine per team member, which four people cannot staff
Services communicate only over the network, so twelve of them will always be too slow to use

rubric: Early boundaries are often wrong and many services add overhead a small team struggles to carry.
Docker works fine with microservices, and monoliths can be decomposed later.

items.prompt: Why does each microservice usually own its own database instead of sharing one schema with the others?

options.label: Separate databases remove most network calls between services, since each one reads its own data
Each service can change its schema and deploy without breaking other services
Separate databases keep data consistent across services, because each one holds its own copy
Each service can skip backups for its own data, since the data is spread across many stores

rubric: Private data ownership keeps services loosely coupled so they deploy independently.
Distractors assume splitting databases removes network calls or guarantees consistency, which it does not.

items.prompt: Which interaction is an example of asynchronous communication between services?

options.label: Search sends an HTTP GET to Catalog and retries until it gets a response back
Orders publishes an OrderPlaced event to a broker and carries on without waiting
Checkout calls the Tax service over REST and waits for the returned tax amount
Cart calls Pricing through a gRPC request and blocks until the reply arrives back

rubric: Publishing an event to a broker lets the sender continue without waiting for consumers.
Distractors are request/response calls where the caller blocks, so they are synchronous.

items.prompt: Order service calls Payment service synchronously with no timeout. Payment becomes very slow. What is the most likely effect on Order service?

options.label: Order service simply skips payment and finishes each request with success
Order requests keep waiting, tying up threads until Order itself becomes slow
Order requests are automatically rerouted to a faster service instance
Order service crashes immediately, so the failure is contained and obvious

rubric: Without timeouts, waiting calls hold resources and the failure cascades to the caller.
Distractors assume automatic rerouting or fast, clean failure, which do not happen by default.

items.prompt: What is the main role of an API gateway in a microservices system?

options.label: It stores each service's data so the services can stay stateless
It builds and packages each service into its own container image
It gives clients one entry point and routes requests to services
It replaces service-to-service messaging by sending all events itself

rubric: A gateway is a single front door that routes and handles cross-cutting concerns for clients.
Distractors confuse it with a database, a build tool, or a message broker.

items.prompt: Which description best fits a well-chosen microservice boundary?

options.label: One service per developer, so each person can deploy their own part
One service per technical layer, such as all controllers in one service
One service per business capability, such as billing, owning its own data
One service per database table, so each table has exactly one owning service

rubric: Boundaries should follow business capabilities so changes stay inside one service.
Splitting by table, layer or person causes chatty calls and tight coupling.

items.prompt: Which of these are genuine benefits that microservices can offer compared with a monolith? Select all that apply.

options.label: Network failures between components no longer need to be handled
A busy service can be scaled without scaling the whole application
Business transactions become simpler because they stay inside one database
Teams can deploy their own service without redeploying everything

rubric: Independent scaling and deployment are core benefits.
Distributed transactions and network failures get harder, not easier, with microservices.

items.prompt: A team split a monolith into Orders, Inventory and Shipping services. They notice that all three must always be released together, and they read and write the same database tables. A colleague asks how to interpret this. What is the best interpretation?

options.label: The services are too small, so they should be split further into functions
The boundaries are wrong, giving a distributed monolith with tight coupling
The team needs more containers, since deploy coupling comes from low capacity
The services are well designed, since shared tables keep data consistent

rubric: Shared tables and lockstep releases mean the services are not independent: a distributed monolith.
Distractors treat the coupling as a good sign or a capacity problem rather than a boundary problem.

items.prompt: A client retries a failed call with exponential backoff: the first retry waits 100 ms and each later wait doubles. How long does it wait before the 4th retry?

options.label: 800 ms
400 ms
300 ms

rubric: Waits are 100, 200, 400, 800 ms, so the 4th retry waits 800 ms.
Other values come from linear growth or counting one step too many.

items.prompt: A circuit breaker around the Recommendations service opens after 5 consecutive failures. The breaker is now open and a 6th request arrives. What happens?

options.label: The call is queued until Recommendations recovers, then replayed
The call is sent to the database of Recommendations directly instead
The call is sent anyway and the breaker closes on a timeout
The call fails immediately without contacting Recommendations

rubric: An open breaker fails fast and spares the struggling service.
Distractors describe sending, queuing or bypassing, which an open breaker does not do.

items.prompt: An order saga runs: reserve inventory, charge payment, schedule shipping. Inventory is reserved, then the payment step fails. What should the saga do next?

options.label: Roll back the Inventory database using a distributed lock on its rows
Retry the inventory reservation until the payment starts to succeed
Run a compensating action that releases the reserved inventory
Leave the reservation in place and mark the order as shipped anyway

rubric: Sagas undo completed steps with compensating actions.
Distractors assume a global rollback or ignore the inconsistency.

items.prompt: A message broker may deliver the same ChargeCustomer message twice. Which change best prevents a double charge?

options.label: Increase the broker's retention so duplicates expire sooner than before
Store each message's idempotency key and ignore any key already processed
Make Payment faster so the second delivery never has time to arrive
Move the Payment code into Orders so only one service sends the message

rubric: Idempotent handling with a stored key makes duplicate delivery harmless.
Distractors try to prevent duplicates rather than tolerate them, which brokers cannot guarantee.

items.prompt: A new feature awards loyalty points per purchase. Following service-boundary rules, where should the points balances be stored?

options.label: In a new Loyalty service that owns its own data store
In the Payment service's existing database tables
In the Orders service's database, beside each order
In the API gateway, which sees every purchase request

rubric: Loyalty is its own business capability, so it should own its data behind an API.
Other options attach it to a service because of where the data originates, creating coupling.

items.prompt: Orders needs the customer's name to print on invoices, but Customer data belongs to the Customer service. Which approaches fit microservice data ownership? Select all that apply.

options.label: Keep a local copy of the name updated from CustomerUpdated events
Query the Customer database tables directly from Orders
Call the Customer service API when the name is needed
Share an ORM library so Orders can open Customer's database

rubric: Using the API or event-fed local copy respects ownership.
Direct database access, even through a shared library, couples the services' schemas.

items.prompt: A checkout endpoint saves the order, then synchronously calls an Email service to send a confirmation. Email is slow, so checkout takes 4 seconds. Customers only need the order saved before seeing success. What change should the team make?

options.label: Publish an OrderPlaced event and let Email consume it in the background
Call Email twice in parallel so one of the calls finishes quickly
Add a larger timeout to the Email call so it waits for each message
Merge Email into Orders so that no network call is involved

rubric: Non-essential work should be moved to an asynchronous event so checkout stays fast.
Longer timeouts, merging, or duplicate calls keep the wait or add new problems.

items.prompt: An order service reserved stock in the inventory service, then the payment service declined the card. Each service has its own database. Using a saga, what is the next step?

options.label: Run a ROLLBACK on the inventory database from the order service
Delete the order row and let the reservation expire on its own
Send a command that releases the inventory reservation
Retry the payment call until it eventually returns success

rubric: A saga undoes a completed local step with a compensating action, here releasing the reservation.
The ROLLBACK distractor assumes a single ACID transaction spans services, which it does not.

items.prompt: A circuit breaker around the pricing service opened after repeated failures, and its 30-second wait has now elapsed. How should it handle the next incoming request?

options.label: Reject all calls until an operator resets it manually
Let a few trial calls through and close if they succeed
Close at once and send full traffic back to the service
Keep failing fast until the failure counter decays to zero

rubric: After the wait, the breaker goes half-open and probes with a few calls before closing.
Closing immediately sends a full load to a service that may still be unhealthy.

items.prompt: A client's POST to a payment service times out, and the client cannot tell whether the charge happened. How should it retry without risking a double charge?

options.label: Send the same idempotency key on each retry so the server dedupes
Switch the call to PUT, which makes any retry safe automatically
Generate a new order ID on every retry so requests stay unique
Shorten the timeout so the retry fires before the charge completes

rubric: Reusing one idempotency key lets the server recognise a repeat and return the original result.
A new ID per retry makes duplicates look like distinct requests.

items.prompt: When an order ships, three other services (email, analytics, loyalty) must react, and the order service must not wait on them. Which design fits?

options.label: Publish an OrderShipped event to a topic that each service subscribes to
Merge the three services into one process so a method call notifies them
Call each of the three services over REST in turn and wait for each 200
Have the three services poll the order database once per second

rubric: Publish-subscribe events decouple the producer from consumers and avoid blocking.
Synchronous calls and DB polling keep the coupling the question asks to remove.

items.prompt: A request passes through three services in sequence. Each is 99.9% available and fails independently. What is the approximate availability of the whole chain?
rubric: Serial availabilities multiply: 0.999^3 is about 0.997.
99.9% ignores the extra dependencies in the chain.

items.prompt: A reporting service needs order data, but the orders service owns its own database. Which approaches respect that ownership? Select all that apply.

options.label: Mount the orders tables into the reporting schema as shared tables
Subscribe to order events and keep a local read model
Pull a paginated export from the orders API on a schedule
Query the orders database directly with read-only credentials

rubric: Events and the owning service's API both access data through the owner's interface.
Direct queries and shared tables couple the reporting service to the orders schema.

items.prompt: The orders API v1 returns an `address` string. A new version must return `street` and `city` instead. Mobile clients on v1 cannot be updated for several weeks. Which rollout step is correct?

options.label: Rename `address` to `street` and `city` now, then notify mobile clients to update
Return both fields but set `address` to null so old clients fail early
Deploy v2 and shut v1 down as soon as the new version passes its tests
Add `street` and `city` while still returning `address`, then remove it later

rubric: An additive, backward-compatible change lets old and new clients work, and the old field is removed after migration.
Renaming or nulling fields breaks existing consumers during the transition.

items.prompt: Traces show checkout latency growing with cart size. For each cart line, checkout makes one sequential HTTP call to the inventory service. Each call is fast, and inventory CPU is low. What is the most likely cause?

options.label: The container image is large, so cold starts delay each request
The service registry is overloaded and slows every call lookup
The inventory database lacks an index, so every query scans a table
Chatty sequential calls add up network latency as the cart grows

rubric: Per-call cost is small, so the per-line sequential calls (N+1 pattern) cause the linear growth; a batch endpoint would help.
Index and cold-start explanations would not scale with cart size.

items.prompt: Billing and Invoicing are separate services, but almost every change touches both, and they must be released in a fixed order. What is the best diagnosis?

options.label: Their REST contracts are too chatty, so moving them to gRPC would decouple the two services
They should share one database so that schema changes no longer need coordinated releases
They are one cohesive capability split too finely, a distributed monolith
Their pipelines are too slow, so faster CI would let the two services deploy in parallel

rubric: Changes and releases that always move together signal a wrong boundary rather than a tooling problem.
A shared database or protocol change would keep or deepen the coupling.

items.prompt: Customers receive duplicate confirmation emails. The consumer sends the email, then acknowledges the message. Logs show some consumers crashing right after sending. What explains the duplicates?

options.label: The email provider retries on its own and creates the copies
Redelivery after a missed ack, with a handler that is not idempotent
Competing consumers on one queue each receive every message
The broker guarantees exactly once, so the producer must publish twice

rubric: A crash before the ack makes the broker redeliver under at-least-once semantics, and a non-idempotent handler resends.
Competing consumers on one queue split messages rather than duplicating them.

items.prompt: In a chain A to B to C to D, each caller retries a failed call 3 times (4 attempts total). When D slows down, D collapses within seconds. Why?

options.label: Short timeouts make D process each request twice before it replies
Retries multiply at each layer, so one request becomes dozens of calls to D
The load balancer pins all traffic to a single D instance, which then overloads
Circuit breakers in every layer stay open and block healthy calls to D, forcing a backlog

rubric: Retry amplification is 4 x 4 x 4 = 64 attempts at D for one user request.
The other options do not match the retry configuration described.

items.prompt: A service commits an order to its database and then publishes an OrderCreated event. Occasionally the order exists but no event was ever sent, and the service was restarted at those times. What is the root cause?

options.label: Several instances publish the same event at once, because no distributed lock guards the publish call
The commit and the publish are separate steps, so a crash between them loses the event
The broker is not durable, so events that were already acknowledged vanish after the broker restarts
The event is published before the commit finishes, so consumers read stale data and drop the event

rubric: A dual write is not atomic; a transactional outbox makes the event durable with the commit.
Broker durability and locking do not explain a missing event after a restart.

items.prompt: Which observations suggest that service boundaries were drawn badly? Select all that apply.

options.label: Each service stores its data in its own database
Each service has its own repository and CI pipeline
Most requests to one service trigger a synchronous call to another to finish
Two services read and write the same database table
A single feature change requires coordinated releases of several services

rubric: Coordinated releases, shared tables and heavy synchronous chaining all indicate high coupling across boundaries.
Separate repositories and private databases are normal features of well-bounded services.

items.prompt: The API gateway times out after 2 seconds, but the order service waits up to 10 seconds on inventory. Users see 504 errors, yet the orders are often created anyway, and frustrated users resubmit them, creating duplicates. What explains this?

options.label: The gateway timeout is shorter than the order service's own processing time, so it must be raised
The downstream timeout exceeds the gateway's, so work continues after the caller gave up
Inventory returns errors on slow calls, and the gateway converts those errors into 504 responses
The order service has no circuit breaker, so failing inventory calls are never cut off early

rubric: Timeouts should shrink down the call chain; otherwise work completes after the caller has already given up, inviting duplicate resubmissions.
Raising the gateway timeout or blaming errors does not explain orders succeeding behind a 504.

items.prompt: Orders calls Inventory synchronously, Inventory calls Pricing, and Pricing calls Orders for discount history. When Pricing slows slightly, all three services stop responding. What best explains the total outage?

options.label: Pricing has run out of database storage, which forces the other two services to crash in sequence
Orders is deployed with too few replicas, so Pricing is flooded with requests that the gateway cannot queue
REST over HTTP cannot carry cross-service traffic reliably, so the services lose connections under load
The call cycle lets slow replies hold request threads in every service, so all thread pools drain at once

rubric: A synchronous cycle propagates latency: each blocked call ties up a thread upstream, causing a cascading failure.
Distractors blame capacity or protocol rather than the dependency structure.

items.prompt: A service saves an order to its database and then publishes an `OrderCreated` event to a broker. Occasionally the order exists but downstream services never hear about it. What is the root cause?

options.label: The event payload is too large, so the broker silently rejects it after the order has committed
The broker uses topics, not queues, so some consumers are never subscribed to the event
The ORM delays the commit until after the publish call returns, which reorders the two steps
The commit and the publish are two separate writes, so a crash between them loses the event

rubric: This is the dual-write problem: no atomicity across the database and the broker; a transactional outbox fixes it.
Other options name plausible but unrelated configuration issues.

items.prompt: After a consumer-group rebalance, a payment service charged some customers twice. The broker guarantees at-least-once delivery and the handler calls the payment gateway directly. Which diagnosis is most accurate?

options.label: The payment gateway retried the call internally after a timeout, and the consumer cannot prevent duplicate charges
The broker produced duplicate copies of messages while the group rebalanced, which is a defect in its delivery logic
The consumer committed offsets too slowly, so the broker concluded the messages were lost and fabricated new ones
Uncommitted messages were redelivered, and the handler has no idempotency check to detect repeats

rubric: At-least-once delivery means redelivery after a rebalance is expected; handlers must be idempotent, e.g. via a dedup key.
Distractors blame the broker or gateway instead of the handler design.

items.prompt: Team A renames a column in a table that Team B's service also reads directly. Team B's service breaks on deploy even though nobody changed B's code. What does this most clearly reveal?

options.label: The migration tool lacked a rollback script, which is the usual cause of cross-team failures
A shared database couples the services' schemas, so one team cannot deploy independently of the other
Team B should have pinned a newer container base image so that the schema change could be absorbed
Team A skipped integration tests, which would have caught the issue regardless of how data is shared

rubric: Sharing a datastore breaks encapsulation; the schema becomes an unversioned API between services.
Other options address process symptoms rather than the structural coupling.

items.prompt: A gateway fans out to 8 services in parallel and waits for all of them. Each service has a p99 of 200 ms, yet the gateway's p99 is around 600 ms. Which explanation best fits?

options.label: The gateway's p99 is measured in a different unit or window, so the figures cannot be compared directly with the services' p99 values
Each service's p99 is inflated by garbage collection pauses, and the gateway's response cache then removes those pauses for repeated requests
The HTTP client executes the parallel calls one after another on a single thread, so the latencies add up on every request
Waiting for the slowest of many parallel calls makes slow outliers show up far more often in the combined response

rubric: Tail latency amplification: with 8 calls, the chance that at least one hits its slow tail is much higher than 1%.
Distractors invent sequential execution or measurement artefacts.

items.prompt: A system split into 12 services is suspected of being a distributed monolith. Which observations support that diagnosis? Select all that apply.

options.label: Each service lives in its own source repository with its own CI pipeline
A single user request triggers dozens of fine-grained calls between two services
Two of the services are written in different programming languages
Services must be deployed in a fixed order or the system breaks
Most features need coordinated changes and releases across three or more services

rubric: Lockstep changes, ordered deploys and chatty calls show strong coupling across boundaries.
Separate repos and mixed languages are organisational and technology choices, not evidence of coupling.

items.prompt: Service B is degraded and handles about half its normal load. Service A calls B and retries each failed call three times immediately, without backoff. Within a minute B stops responding entirely, even though the original traffic did not increase. What is the most accurate analysis?

options.label: The retries multiplied the load on an already struggling B, pushing it from degraded to fully down
B should return HTTP 200 on failures, because error codes make clients retry more aggressively and add load to B
B's autoscaler is misconfigured, and A's retries have no real effect on how much load B receives overall
A's retries succeed too often, which fills B's caches with stale entries until B can no longer serve requests

rubric: Immediate retries amplify load up to 4x on a dependency that is already short on capacity (retry storm).
Distractors blame unrelated mechanisms or misread how error codes drive retries.

items.prompt: A checkout workflow spans six services with compensating actions. Criteria: the flow changes monthly, support needs to see exactly which step a failed order is stuck on, and teams want to avoid services knowing each other's events. Which saga style fits best?

options.label: Orchestration, where a coordinator owns the flow and its state, so changes and step visibility sit in one place
Choreography, where each service reacts to events and emits its own, so no central component is needed
Choreography with a shared event schema package that every service imports to follow the steps
A two-phase commit across all six databases, so every step commits or aborts together at one point

rubric: Orchestration centralises flow logic and state, meeting the change and visibility criteria and keeping services unaware of each other.
Choreography spreads the flow across services, making it hard to see and change.

items.prompt: A dashboard needs data from Orders, Customers and Shipping. Criteria: it is read about 500 times per second, staleness of a few seconds is acceptable, and it must stay available if Shipping is down. Which design is best?

options.label: Cache every response in the browser for one hour, so the services are rarely called at all
Build a read model fed by events from the three services, so the dashboard queries only its own store
Call the three services synchronously per request and merge results in the dashboard backend
Query the three services' databases directly through a shared read-only account to avoid network hops

rubric: An event-fed read model gives fast reads and independence from Shipping's availability, and the allowed staleness fits eventual consistency.
Per-request composition ties availability to all three services; direct DB access breaks ownership.

items.prompt: You are choosing the first module to extract from a monolith. Criteria: highest change frequency, clear ownership of its own data, and few inbound calls from other modules. Which candidate is best?

options.label: Reporting, which changes rarely and joins data from every other module in nightly batch queries
Core pricing, which changes weekly but shares four tables with billing, inventory and promotions
Product search, which changes often, owns its index, and is called by only the web front end
User accounts, which are read by nearly every module but change only a few times a year

rubric: Search meets all three criteria: high churn, owned data, low coupling.
Other candidates fail on coupling, shared data or low change rate.

items.prompt: A proposal uses two-phase commit across the Orders, Payments and Inventory databases for checkout. Which critique is strongest given goals of high availability and independent deployment?

options.label: Locks are held while waiting on the slowest participant, and a coordinator failure can block all of them
Two-phase commit is unsafe because it can commit only some of the participants' changes at the end
Two-phase commit needs a message broker, and brokers cannot be used for transactional work
Two-phase commit forbids retries, which means that transient network errors always abort the order

rubric: 2PC holds locks across services and blocks on coordinator or participant failure, hurting availability and autonomy.
Distractors misstate 2PC's atomicity or its relationship to brokers and retries.

items.prompt: You configure a circuit breaker on calls to a flaky recommendations service. Criteria: protect the caller's threads, keep the product page usable, and detect recovery within about 30 seconds. Which configuration is best?

options.label: Open after the first failure and stay open until an engineer resets it after reviewing the logs and confirming the fix
Open after repeated failures, return a default list, and probe with a few trial calls every 30 seconds
Never open the breaker, but raise the timeout to 30 seconds so slow calls have time to finish
Open after repeated failures and fail the whole page with an error, so users know to retry a little later

rubric: Opening on failures, falling back, and half-open probing protects threads, degrades gracefully and detects recovery.
Long timeouts tie up threads; manual reset ignores recovery; failing the page ignores usability.

items.prompt: A five-person team plans to launch a new product as 40 microservices from day one. Which criticisms are well-founded? Select all that apply.

options.label: Containers cannot run more than ten services on one cluster without losing isolation
Most calls will cross the network, so latency and partial failures will occur far more often
Boundaries are guessed before the domain is understood, so they will likely need costly redrawing
The operational load of deployment, monitoring and tracing for 40 services will swamp five people
Microservices cannot be written by a team smaller than the number of services it owns

rubric: Premature boundaries, operational overhead and network failure modes are real costs at this team size.
The last two claims are false: there is no such team-size rule and no such container limit.

items.prompt: Your Customer service must replace the field `phone` with `phones[]`. Unknown consumers, including some mobile app versions that cannot be force-updated, read `phone`. Criteria: no breaking of existing consumers, and eventual removal of the old field. Which plan is best?

options.label: Replace `phone` with `phones[]` now and publish release notes, since consumers are responsible for tracking changes
Rename the service endpoint to `/v2` and delete `/v1` after one week, since unused versions add risk
Add `phones[]` alongside `phone`, keep both populated, track usage of `phone`, then remove it once usage ends
Keep `phone` forever and never add `phones[]`, so no consumer ever needs to change its code

rubric: Expand-and-contract keeps old clients working while measuring usage, allowing safe removal later.
Other options break clients, block the change, or remove the old version too soon.

items.prompt: A checkout flow spans nine services with conditional branches and compensations. Auditors need one place to see each order's current step and why it failed. Judged against these criteria, which saga style fits best?

options.label: Choreography with a shared state table, since every service can then read and update the flow state directly
Orchestration, since one coordinator holds the flow state and compensations, so status and failures can be queried
Two-phase commit, since it gives auditors one atomic transaction record across all nine services and their databases
Choreography, since services reacting to each other's events need no central component and keep the flow easy to trace

rubric: An orchestrator centralises flow state and compensation logic, which satisfies the visibility and audit criteria for a complex branching flow.
Choreography scatters the flow across services, and a shared table or 2PC would break service autonomy.

items.prompt: A team proposes letting the reporting service query the orders service's read replica directly, to avoid building and maintaining an API. Which critique of this proposal is most sound?

options.label: Replication lag makes the data stale, so the proposal is acceptable once the replica is configured for synchronous replication
Services should exchange data through message brokers, so a direct query is a problem because it is a synchronous call
It couples reporting to the orders schema, so table changes in orders can break reporting and block independent deployment
A read-only replica cannot be modified by reporting, so the data stays safe and the two services remain loosely coupled

rubric: Reading another service's tables makes its schema a hidden public contract, which defeats independent deployability.
Read-only access and replication lag are not the core issue; the coupling is.

items.prompt: Service A calls B, B calls C, and C calls D, and each caller makes up to 3 attempts in total (the first call plus 2 retries) when a call fails. D degrades and begins to time out. Which assessment of this retry design is best?

options.label: Sound, since retrying at every layer gives each request the best chance of succeeding while D recovers from its problem
Sound, provided each layer waits a fixed one second between attempts, since spacing the retries out stops load from compounding at D
Flawed, since retries add load to a failing service, so every layer should drop retries and rely on much longer timeouts instead
Flawed, since nested retries multiply to as many as 27 calls at D; retry at one layer with a budget and backoff

rubric: Stacked retries multiply (3x3x3) and push a degraded dependency into collapse; a single retry layer with budgets limits this.
Retrying everywhere or lengthening timeouts does not stop amplification.

items.prompt: A company runs 12 services. Which observation is the strongest evidence that it has built a distributed monolith rather than true microservices?

options.label: Most releases require several services to deploy together in a set order because their changes depend on each other
Some services call each other over HTTP synchronously, so a slow downstream service can delay the response the user is waiting for
Each service has its own repository and CI pipeline even though engineers often review code across teams and share some conventions
All services are written in one language and share a common logging library maintained by a platform team

rubric: Lockstep deployment shows the services are not independently deployable, the defining property that is lost in a distributed monolith.
Shared language, sync calls and separate repos are compatible with healthy microservices.

items.prompt: The orders service must tell six downstream consumers that an order was placed. Some consumers are often offline for maintenance, and order acceptance must never be blocked by them. Which approach best meets these criteria?

options.label: Call all six consumers over REST in sequence, so each response confirms that consumer has processed the order before acceptance completes
Let each consumer poll the orders database every minute, so the orders service does not need to run a broker or publish a contract
Call all six over REST in parallel with a 30-second timeout, so a slow or offline consumer delays acceptance for at most that timeout
Publish an OrderPlaced event to a durable broker, so consumers catch up after downtime without blocking acceptance

rubric: A durable event decouples availability and time, so offline consumers catch up later while orders are still accepted.
Synchronous calls, even parallel, tie acceptance to consumer availability; polling the database couples to the schema.

items.prompt: A proposal splits a system into a UI service, a business-logic service and a data-access service. Which criticisms of this decomposition are valid? Select all that apply.

options.label: The layered services cannot be containerised, since a Docker image cannot hold only one layer of an application
Each request needs a chain of network hops, adding latency and failure points that business-aligned services would avoid
Splitting by layer ignores business capabilities, so no team can deliver a complete feature independently
Almost every feature change touches all three services, so they must be changed and released together
Each service's data is owned by exactly one team, which makes ownership too clear to be useful

rubric: Layer-based splits create cross-service change coupling, extra hops and no end-to-end team ownership.
Clear data ownership is a benefit, and containerisation is unaffected by layering.

items.prompt: A startup with 7 engineers runs a monolith that deploys several times a day with little pain or scaling pressure. A new CTO wants 15 services for 'scalability'. Domain boundaries are still shifting each quarter. Judged on cost and risk, what is the best recommendation?

options.label: Split into 15 services that share one database, since that removes consistency work while keeping deployments independent
Rewrite everything as services in one big-bang effort, since that avoids running two architectures in parallel for long
Keep a modular monolith with enforced module boundaries, and extract a service only when a concrete scaling or team need appears
Split now along current guesses, since early boundaries are cheap to change once services exist and teams adapt

rubric: With shifting boundaries and no pain, a modular monolith avoids premature distribution costs while preserving future extraction options.
Wrong boundaries are costly to fix across services, and a shared database defeats the purpose.

items.prompt: Requirement: when an order row is saved, an OrderPlaced event must be published, with no lost events and no events for unsaved orders, even if the service crashes at any point. Which design meets it?

options.label: Wrap the save and publish in a try block and delete the order row if the publish throws any error
Insert the order and an outbox row in one local transaction; a relay publishes outbox rows and marks them sent
Publish to the broker first, then save the order, so only a failed save needs any manual cleanup afterwards
Save the order, then publish to the broker on the next line, retrying the publish from in-memory state on failure

rubric: The transactional outbox makes state change and event intent atomic; the relay gives at-least-once delivery.
The other designs leave a crash window between the database write and the publish.

items.prompt: Service P renames `cust_id` to `customerId` in its response. Consumers X, Y and Z deploy on their own schedules. You need zero downtime and no coordinated release. Which plan meets these constraints?

options.label: Release a v2 and shut v1 off immediately, since a version bump counts as backward compatible for existing callers
Rename the field now and email consumers, since consumers must keep up with the provider's current contract
Return both fields, let consumers migrate at their own pace under contract tests, then drop the old one
Schedule one release window for the provider and all three consumers, so only one form of the field exists

rubric: Expand and contract with consumer contract tests allows independent migration with no downtime.
Renaming, shutting off v1 or a synchronised release each break the constraints.

items.prompt: A product page needs data from catalogue, pricing and inventory services, with p99 latency under 100 ms, and it must still render if one of those services is down. Which design meets all constraints?

options.label: An API composer calling all three services synchronously per request, since fresh data matters more than latency
A browser that calls the three services in sequence, since the page can show whatever data arrives first
A shared database view joining the three services' tables, since a join is the fastest way to combine their data
A read model built from events of the three services, served from its own store, with staleness tolerated on some fields

rubric: A CQRS-style read model gives low latency and resilience to individual outages at the cost of eventual consistency.
Sync composition and shared views fail the availability or ownership constraints.

items.prompt: A booking saga has three steps: reserve seat, charge card, send confirmation email. The email cannot be unsent; the reservation and charge can be compensated. Which design is best?

options.label: Send the email first, since the customer gets immediate feedback and an apology email can compensate if a later step fails
Charge first, then email, then reserve, since payment is the riskiest step and the email only needs to follow a successful charge
Reserve, charge, then send the email last, since the irreversible step should run only after all compensable steps have succeeded
Run all three steps in parallel, since this shortens the saga and compensating transactions can undo whichever steps fail

rubric: Irreversible steps should come last, after the point where failure and compensation are still possible.
Sending early or in parallel exposes customers to irreversible, possibly wrong, messages.

items.prompt: Service G calls a slow dependency S and a fast dependency T from one shared pool of 50 threads. When S slows down, G also stops serving requests that only need T. Which change meets the goal of keeping T paths healthy?

options.label: Add retries to every S call, so slow calls are repeated until they complete and release the shared threads
Raise the shared pool to 500 threads, so S can consume more without ever starving the T paths of capacity
Give S and T separate bounded pools, with a timeout and circuit breaker on S so its failures fail fast
Run S calls on the same thread as T calls, so that a slow call blocks only the single current request

rubric: Bulkheads isolate resource pools, and timeouts with circuit breaking stop S from consuming resources indefinitely.
Bigger pools or retries only delay exhaustion or add load.

items.prompt: You design a consumer on an at-least-once broker that must charge a customer only once per `paymentId`. Which elements belong in the design? Select all that apply.

options.label: Use a unique constraint on `paymentId`, so concurrent duplicate deliveries cannot both commit the effect
Record the processed `paymentId` in the same local transaction as the charge effect, so duplicates are detected
Acknowledge the message before processing, so the broker never redelivers and duplicates become impossible
Derive the idempotency key from the event's business ID, not from a random value generated on each attempt
Keep processed IDs only in process memory, since restarts are rare and redelivery usually follows restarts

rubric: Idempotency needs a stable business key and atomic, durable deduplication tied to the effect.
Acking early risks lost work, and in-memory IDs vanish on restart.

items.prompt: A monolith and its shared Postgres database serve orders and billing. You must move billing data into its own service with no downtime, no big-bang cutover, and the ability to roll back at each stage. Which plan meets all three constraints?

options.label: Create the new service reading the monolith's billing tables directly, then move callers over one at a time and drop the old billing code once all are moved
Route billing calls through a facade, sync data to the new store via change data capture, verify parity, then shift reads and writes gradually
Rewrite billing in the new service with an empty database, send all new traffic there at once, and backfill historical records from the monolith later
Freeze writes for a weekend, copy the billing tables into a new database, verify the copy, and then switch every caller to the new service

rubric: A facade with continuous sync and parity checks allows gradual, reversible migration without downtime.
The other plans need downtime, keep the shared database, or lose existing data and rollback ability.
